title: MASAI randomized trial in southwest Sweden: Transpara-supported mammography screening finds more cancers with less screen reading, at a non-inferior interval cancer rate
summary: In the MASAI trial of 105,934 women, Transpara-supported screening found 6.4 cancers per 1,000 against 5.0 with standard double reading. It cut screen reading by 44.2%.
headline: *Transpara* helps Swedish breast screening find more cancers
metric: a detection rate of 6.4 per 1,000 against 5.0 per 1,000
brief: Lund University researchers ran the MASAI trial within the Swedish national screening program. Between 12 April 2021 and 7 December 2022, they randomly assigned 105,934 women in southwest Sweden to Transpara-supported screening or to a control group. In the control group, two radiologists without AI did standard double reading. The AI group had 6.4 screen-detected cancers per 1,000 women against 5.0 in the control group. It needed 44.2% fewer screen readings.[1] Results for the primary outcome, the rate of interval cancers, appeared in The Lancet in 2026. The rate was 1.55 per 1,000 with AI and 1.76 per 1,000 without. That result met the trial's non-inferiority margin. The difference was not statistically significant.[2] The trial tested one product in one region. Its design does not separate the effect of the triage by risk score from that of the marks on suspicious areas.[3]

title: ScreenTrustCAD at Capio Sankt Göran Hospital, Stockholm: Lunit Insight MMG as a third reader leads to 19 more screen-detected breast cancers than two radiologists
summary: In Stockholm, Lunit's Insight MMG read 55,581 mammograms beside two radiologists, and the three together found 269 cancers against 250 by the radiologists alone.
headline: *Insight MMG* as a third reader finds more breast cancers in Stockholm
metric: the three together found 269 cancers against 250 by the radiologists alone
brief: The ScreenTrustCAD study measured what an AI reader adds where breast screening already uses two radiologists.[1] Karolinska Institutet researchers ran it at Capio Sankt Göran Hospital in Stockholm. From 1 April 2021 to 9 June 2022, Lunit's Insight MMG ran in the background on the screening mammograms of 55,581 women. Two radiologists alone would have found 250 cancers. With the AI as a third reader, 269 were found. In the paired design, two radiologists and the AI read the examinations independently. The 19 extra cancers therefore came from examinations that only the AI flagged.[2] The researchers also found that one radiologist with AI was non-inferior to two radiologists, with 261 cancers against 250. The study ran at one hospital with one mammography vendor. Lunit was among its funders.[3]

brief: On 4 February 2020 BenevolentAI researchers reported in The Lancet that their knowledge graph had helped them identify a possible treatment for COVID-19. It was baricitinib, an arthritis drug. In the ACTT-2 trial, 1,033 hospitalized adults received remdesivir with either baricitinib or a placebo. Median recovery took 7 days with baricitinib and 8 days with the placebo. In the COV-BARRIER trial, 8% of patients receiving baricitinib had died by day 28, compared with 13% receiving a placebo. Mortality was a secondary outcome in that trial. The trial did not meet its primary outcome of reduced disease progression.[1] In the later RECOVERY trial, 8,156 patients were randomly assigned to usual care with or without baricitinib. Mortality, its primary outcome, was 12% with baricitinib and 14% with usual care alone.[2] On 14 January 2022 the World Health Organization strongly recommended baricitinib with corticosteroids. The recommendation covered patients severely or critically ill with COVID-19. On 10 May 2022 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved baricitinib for hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who need supplemental oxygen or other respiratory support. The European Medicines Agency reached the provisional opinion that three trials did not conclusively show meaningful benefit. Eli Lilly then withdrew its European application on 7 December 2022.[3] None of the trials compared discovery with AI against discovery without it. The knowledge graph's part in the choice rests on a letter and a methods paper by BenevolentAI researchers.[4]

title: Zasocitinib, designed by Nimbus with Schrödinger's computational platform, clears psoriasis in more trial patients than deucravacitinib. It gains priority review from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration
summary: Takeda reports 36.5% complete skin clearance with zasocitinib versus 13.9% with deucravacitinib at week 16 for a drug that Nimbus designed with Schrödinger's computational platform.
headline: Zasocitinib clears psoriasis in more patients than deucravacitinib
metric: 36.5% complete skin clearance with zasocitinib versus 13.9% with deucravacitinib at week 16
brief: In the LATITUDE Atlas phase 3 trial, 36.5% of 301 participants on zasocitinib reached complete skin clearance at week 16. On deucravacitinib, 13.9% of 303 participants did so. Takeda reports these figures.[1] Takeda also reports that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted priority review to its application. No approval had been reported by 29 October 2026.[2] A Cochrane meta-analysis by Sbidian and colleagues, published on 6 August 2025, included an earlier phase 2b trial of zasocitinib. The authors rated the certainty of evidence as low for most comparisons that involve the drug. They declare no ties to Takeda or Nimbus.[3] The attribution to AI is weaker. Nimbus and Schrödinger developed zasocitinib with computational structure-based design. Schrödinger describes free-energy calculations and virtual screening. The approach was AI-assisted, according to a Takeda scientist interviewed in Drug Target Review in 2025.[4] None of these accounts isolates the effect of AI from the rest of the discovery work. Takeda announced an upfront payment of approximately $4 billion for the program when the acquisition closed in 2023.[5] That payment is no measure of the effect of AI.

comparator_after: 36.5% of patients (n = 301) achieving PASI 100 at week 16

title: Veterans Health Administration cluster-randomized rollout of GI Genius: Adenoma detection rises from 50.7% to 54.9% at equipped facilities
summary: At 42 VA facilities chosen at random to receive GI Genius, adenoma detection rose from 50.7% to 54.9%, while it fell from 51.8% to 51.1% at 97 control facilities.
headline: *GI Genius* lifts adenoma detection in VA colonoscopy units
metric: adenoma detection rose from 50.7% to 54.9%
brief: The Veterans Health Administration tested computer-aided polyp detection in routine colonoscopy at scale.[1] It assigned facilities at random to receive a device for polyp detection. The device is listed in the trial registry as Medtronic's GI Genius. At 42 equipped facilities adenoma detection rose from 50.7% to 54.9%. At 97 control facilities it fell from 51.8% to 51.1%. Withdrawal time did not change. The gain was 4.2 percentage points on a baseline that was already about 51%. The rate of 54.9% rests on 35,399 colonoscopies. The Veterans Health Administration program that installed the devices also ran and reported the study.[2] The authors state that the effect on cancer outcomes remains unknown. They add that the risk that endoscopists lose skill remains unknown too. Elsewhere, researchers found a gain in a randomized trial at two Seoul hospitals and no gain in another at a Japanese community hospital.
